power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: People with mental disorders have shortened life expectancy, but much evidence on excess mortality comes from specialist psychiatric populations.
We examined variation across the broader diagnosed population by clinical context and time since diagnosis.
Methods: We followed 5,526,599 Finnish residents aged 5-95 years without recorded mental disorders at entry from 2011 to 2023 (63 million person-years).
ICD-11-grouped diagnoses and mortality rate ratios (MRRs) were assessed by time since diagnosis, psychiatric care setting, substance use disorder (SUD) status, age, and cause of death.
Results: During follow-up, 1,463,064 individuals (26.5%) received a diagnosis; the overall adjusted MRR was 2.65 (95% CI 2.53-2.77).
However, among diagnosed individuals aged 5-64 years, 46.1% belonged to a subgroup with rapidly declining excess mortality and little evidence of excess beyond two years.
This subgroup had depressive, anxiety or fearrelated, or stress-related disorders without diagnosed SUD or specialist psychiatric care during follow-up.
At two years, MRRs ranged from 0.88 (95% CI 0.73-1.06) to 1.04 (0.88-1.22) in men and 0.92 (0.79-1.07) to 1.12 (0.96-1.31) in women.
Excess mortality persisted in specialist care and was particularly high with SUD.
It also persisted without SUD or specialist care in schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders and older adults with depression.
Conclusions: Excess mortality after mental disorder diagnosis may be transient in large parts of the diagnosed population while remaining persistent in others with the same diagnosis.
Recognizing these differences is important for interpreting mortality estimates 52 and communicating prognosis across health care.
People with mental disorders are commonly reported to live 7-15 years less than the general population, making premature mortality a major public health concern in psychiatry [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: People with mental disorders are commonly reported to live 7-15 years less than the general population, making premature mortality a major public health concern in psychiatry <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Population-based evidence, however, suggests that the lifetime probability of receiving a mental disorder diagnosis may approach 70-80% [4] [5] [6], while much of the evidence on excess mortality has been derived from specialist psychiatric populations [1] [2] [3] 7].
text.formatted: Population-based evidence, however, suggests that the lifetime probability of receiving a mental disorder diagnosis may approach 70-80% <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, while much of the evidence on excess mortality has been derived from specialist psychiatric populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: What, then, does a single mortality gap tell us about prognosis across the broad population with mental disorders?
Depressive, anxiety, and stress-related disorders are among the most common mental disorders, yet estimates of their associated mortality vary markedly across studies.

Recent meta-analyses report increased mortality across these disorders and particularly high mortality shortly after depression diagnosis, but also substantial unexplained heterogeneity in risk estimates [8, 9].
text.formatted: Recent meta-analyses report increased mortality across these disorders and particularly high mortality shortly after depression diagnosis, but also substantial unexplained heterogeneity in risk estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Two potentially important dimensions of this clinical context are clinical setting and comorbid substance use disorder (SUD) [10, 11].
text.formatted: Two potentially important dimensions of this clinical context are clinical setting and comorbid substance use disorder (SUD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: Both identify populations with substantially different clinical characteristics and mortality risk, but these differences are obscured by average diagnosis-specific estimates.

Establishing whether excess mortality persists across the broader diagnosed population or is concentrated in particular clinical groups and periods after diagnosis is important for understanding the mortality gap and for informing patients and clinicians about how mortality risk changes after diagnosis.

We therefore used nationwide data covering both primary and specialist care to examine excess mortality across ICD-11 mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorder groups according to age, psychiatric care setting, comorbid SUD, cause of death, and time since diagnosis.
We further estimated absolute survival loss over ten years.
Our aim was to determine whether excess mortality persists broadly across the diagnosed population or varies according to clinical context and time since diagnosis.
This nationwide register-based cohort study included all individuals aged 5-95 years residing in Finland between January 1, 2011, and December 31, 2023.
Individuals with prevalent mental disorders before cohort entry were excluded.
Participants were followed from cohort entry until death, permanent emigration, or end of follow-up on Dec 31, 2023, whichever occurred first.

Diagnoses recorded using ICD-8, ICD-9, or the International Classification of Primary Care, Second Edition were converted to corresponding ICD-10 categories, and register data were preprocessed to maximize diagnostic consistency across data sources and classification systems [13].
text.formatted: Diagnoses recorded using ICD-8, ICD-9, or the International Classification of Primary Care, Second Edition were converted to corresponding ICD-10 categories, and register data were preprocessed to maximize diagnostic consistency across data sources and classification systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorders were then classified according to ICD-11 groupings using WHO ICD-10-to-ICD-11 mapping tables.
Mutually exclusive groupings were created using 10to11MapToOneCategory mappings (see Supplementary Methods).
Follow-up was split according to time-varying covariates using a Lexis approach.

Age was split into 5-year bands (1-year bands for age-specific analyses), time since diagnosis at 0.25, 0.5, 1, and 2 years and at 2-year intervals thereafter through 10 years, and calendar time at January 1, 2015, and January 1, 2020.
Gender was obtained from the population register and classified as man or woman according to legal gender recorded in administrative registers.
Region was classified into 5 Finnish collaborative areas for health care and social welfare services.
Physical comorbidity was measured using the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), a weighted index of chronic medical conditions [14].
text.formatted: Physical comorbidity was measured using the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), a weighted index of chronic medical conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Scores were calculated from ICD-10 diagnoses recorded in specialist care during the 5 years before cohort entry and categorized as 0, 1 to 3, or 4 or greater [15].
text.formatted: Scores were calculated from ICD-10 diagnoses recorded in specialist care during the 5 years before cohort entry and categorized as 0, 1 to 3, or 4 or greater <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Age was excluded from the CCI because it was adjusted for separately.
The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, obtained from Statistics Finland's Cause of Death Register.
Cause-specific deaths were classified as natural or external according to the national classification of causes of death.
External deaths included suicides, assaults, and accidents; deaths with missing cause-of-death information were classified separately.
Person-time was aggregated across exposure states, covariates, and time scales.
Mortality rates and mortality rate ratios (MRRs) with 95% CIs were estimated using Poisson regression with log person-years as the offset and robust standard errors.
The basic model adjusted for age band, calendar period, region, and gender; the second model additionally adjusted for CCI category.
MRRs were also estimated according to psychiatric care setting and SUD status, separately for women and men.
We estimated MRRs for all mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorders combined and by ICD-11 diagnostic group.
Diagnosis-specific analyses compared individuals with each diagnosis with all individuals without that specific diagnosis, including those with other mental disorder diagnoses.
Age-specific MRRs were estimated using natural cubic splines for age (4 degrees of freedom, selected by visual inspection of model fit).
We compared estimates based on specialist psychiatric diagnoses with those including primary and specialist care to examine the influence of case ascertainment across age.

Analyses according to psychiatric care setting and SUD status were conducted separately for ages 5-64 and 65-95 years because of differences in underlying mortality and disorder distribution; analyses for older individuals are reported in the Supplement.
Individuals with SUD before the diagnosis of interest were classified in the corresponding SUD state at diagnosis.

Changes in excess mortality after diagnosis were modeled using interactions between exposure state and natural cubic splines for time since diagnosis (3 degrees of freedom), with model-predicted MRRs evaluated on a 0.1-year grid.
Ten-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) was estimated from CCI-adjusted Poisson models including interactions between exposure state and time since diagnosis.
Differences in RMST between individuals with and without each diagnostic group were used to quantify absolute differences in predicted survival during the first ten years after diagnosis.
CIs were estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling with 200 iterations.
Causespecific RMST differences were estimated separately for natural and external deaths.
Additional analyses restricted incident disorders to 2016 onward to reduce potential prevalent-case misclassification and repeated analyses using ICD-10 main diagnostic groups.
Analyses were conducted from February through August 2026 using R version 4.4.3 (R Core Team).
ChatGPT (OpenAI; https://chatgpt.com) was used to assist with developing and debugging R code and improving the readability and language of the manuscript.
text.formatted: ChatGPT (OpenAI; <ref type="url" target="https://chatgpt.com">https://chatgpt.com</ref>) was used to assist with developing and debugging R code and improving the readability and language of the manuscript.

text.text: The authors reviewed and verified the analyses and retained responsibility for the final manuscript.
A total of 5 526 599 individuals (2 784 897 [50.4%] women) were followed for 63 million person-years.
During follow-up, 1 463 064 (26.5%) received at least one mental, behavioural, or neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, including 837 323 (30.1%) women and 625 741 (22.8%) men.
SUD was diagnosed in 119 024 (4.3%) men and 58 859 (2.1%) women.
Numbers of individuals and mortality rates according to diagnosis, age groups, gender, psychiatric care setting, SUD status, and model covariates are presented in Supplementary Tables S1-S5.
text.formatted: Numbers of individuals and mortality rates according to diagnosis, age groups, gender, psychiatric care setting, SUD status, and model covariates are presented in Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1-S5</ref>.

text.text: Depressive disorders, anxiety or fear-related disorders, and disorders specifically associated with stress were the three most common diagnostic groups overall (Table 1) and were commonly recorded outside specialist psychiatric care (Supplementary Table S1).
text.formatted: Depressive disorders, anxiety or fear-related disorders, and disorders specifically associated with stress were the three most common diagnostic groups overall (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>) and were commonly recorded outside specialist psychiatric care (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: Among individuals aged 5-64 years with a mental disorder, 861 842 (75.3%) had at least one of these three disorders.
Of these, 527 905 had neither a diagnosed SUD nor specialist psychiatric care during follow-up, accounting for 46.1% of all individuals with a mental disorder in this age group.
Among individuals aged 65-95 years, dementia and depressive disorders were the most common diagnostic groups (Supplementary Table S2).
text.formatted: Among individuals aged 65-95 years, dementia and depressive disorders were the most common diagnostic groups (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Excess mortality varied across ICD-11 diagnostic groups (Table 1).
text.formatted: Excess mortality varied across ICD-11 diagnostic groups (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Adjustment for baseline physical comorbidity reduced MRRs, but substantial variation across diagnostic groups remained.

Among diagnostic groups with stable estimates, SUD had the highest adjusted MRR (3.23, 95% CI, 3.04-3.44), whereas MRRs were lower for depressive disorders (1.55, 1.48-1.62), anxiety or fear-related disorders (1.41, 1.34-1.49), and disorders specifically associated with stress (1.48, 1.39-1.57).
MRRs also varied substantially with age and case ascertainment (Figure 1).
text.formatted: MRRs also varied substantially with age and case ascertainment (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Restricting diagnoses to specialist psychiatric care produced higher MRRs at younger ages but lower MRRs at older ages than ascertainment from both primary and specialist care.

Across all mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorders combined, MRRs were highest immediately after diagnosis and declined during the first two years across all clinical subgroups (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Across all mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorders combined, MRRs were highest immediately after diagnosis and declined during the first two years across all clinical subgroups (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: Excess mortality nevertheless remained elevated overall throughout follow-up, with the highest MRRs among individuals with SUD receiving specialist psychiatric care and the lowest among those without SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care.

Temporal patterns were similar for natural and external causes, although relative mortality was higher for external causes, particularly among individuals with SUD receiving specialist psychiatric care.
Follow-up-averaged MRRs according to diagnostic group, SUD status, and psychiatric care setting are presented separately for individuals aged 5-64 and 65-95 years in Supplementary Tables S6 and S7.
text.formatted: Follow-up-averaged MRRs according to diagnostic group, SUD status, and psychiatric care setting are presented separately for individuals aged 5-64 and 65-95 years in Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">S6</ref> and <ref type="table">S7</ref>.

text.text: Mortality trajectories varied substantially not only across diagnostic groups but also within diagnostic groups according to SUD status, psychiatric care setting, and age (Figures 3 and 4).
text.formatted: Mortality trajectories varied substantially not only across diagnostic groups but also within diagnostic groups according to SUD status, psychiatric care setting, and age (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref>).

text.text: Among individuals aged 5-64 years with depressive, anxiety or fear-related, or stressrelated disorders who had no diagnosed SUD and were treated outside specialist psychiatric care-46.1% of all individuals with a mental disorder in this age group-MRRs declined rapidly after diagnosis.

At two years, MRRs ranged from 0.88 (95% CI 0.73-1.06) to 1.04 (0.88-1.22) in men and from 0.92 (0.79-1.07) to 1.12 (0.96-1.31) in women across these three diagnostic groups, with little evidence of excess mortality thereafter.

For these disorders, excess mortality was more persistent among individuals receiving specialist psychiatric care, whereas among those with SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care it declined substantially over time.
Similar temporal patterns were observed among individuals aged 65-95 years, although for depressive disorders excess mortality persisted across all clinical subgroups.
Schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders showed a different pattern, with excess mortality persisting even among individuals without SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care.
Time-varying MRRs for the remaining diagnostic groups, including cause-specific estimates, are presented in Supplementary Figures S1-S14.
text.formatted: Time-varying MRRs for the remaining diagnostic groups, including cause-specific estimates, are presented in Supplementary Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S1-S14</ref>.

text.text: Differences in relative mortality were also reflected in absolute survival (Supplementary Tables S8 and S9).
text.formatted: Differences in relative mortality were also reflected in absolute survival (Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">S8</ref> and <ref type="table">S9</ref>).

text.text: Among individuals without SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care, ten-year survival loss was small for depressive disorders (0.09 years in men and 0.05 in women), anxiety or fear-related disorders (0.03 and 0.01 years, respectively), and stressrelated disorders (0.01 and -0.01 years).
Thus, for these common disorders, estimated survival loss in this clinical group was generally measured in days rather than months.

Among individuals with SUD receiving specialist psychiatric care, the corresponding differences were substantially larger: 0.67 years in men and 0.43 years in women for depressive disorders, 0.45 and 0.27 years, respectively, for anxiety or fear-related disorders, and 0.59 and 0.39 for stress-related disorders.

Across all mental, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental disorders, ten-year survival loss was 0.53 years in men and 0.34 years in women, with survival loss associated with natural causes substantially greater than that associated with external causes of death.
The corresponding RMST estimates for individuals with and without each diagnostic group are presented in Supplementary Tables S10 and S11.

text.text: Results were similar when analyses were restricted to disorders first diagnosed from 2016 onward (Figure S15).
text.formatted: Results were similar when analyses were restricted to disorders first diagnosed from 2016 onward (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S15</ref>).

text.text: Using ICD-10 main diagnostic groups resulted in more individuals being classified as having a mental disorder than using the ICD-11 grouping (32.0% vs 26.5%) and yielded lower MRRs for mental disorders combined, particularly when diagnoses outside specialist psychiatric care were included; estimates based solely on specialist psychiatric care were similar (Supplementary Tables S12 and S13).
text.formatted: Using ICD-10 main diagnostic groups resulted in more individuals being classified as having a mental disorder than using the ICD-11 grouping (32.0% vs 26.5%) and yielded lower MRRs for mental disorders combined, particularly when diagnoses outside specialist psychiatric care were included; estimates based solely on specialist psychiatric care were similar (Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S12</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S13</ref>).

text.text: In this nationwide study, excess mortality associated with mental disorders differed markedly according to clinical context and time since diagnosis.

Among individuals aged 5-64 years, those with depressive, anxiety or fear-related, or stress-related disorders who had no diagnosed SUD and did not receive specialist psychiatric care during follow-up accounted for over 46% of all individuals with a mental disorder.
In this large group, mortality was elevated immediately after diagnosis but declined rapidly during the first two years, with little evidence of excess mortality thereafter.
In contrast, excess mortality was more persistent among individuals receiving specialist psychiatric care and particularly high after diagnosis among those with SUD.
Schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders showed a different pattern, with excess mortality persisting even among individuals without SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care.

A single followup-averaged mortality estimate for a diagnostic group therefore obscures a central feature of the mortality gap: excess mortality may be transient in a large part of the diagnosed population while remaining substantial or persistent in others with the same diagnosis.

Distinguishing when and in whom excess mortality occurs is important for better targeting preventive efforts and for giving patients and clinicians a more informative account of how mortality risk changes after diagnosis.

Previous studies have shown that excess mortality following depression, anxiety, and stress-related disorders is highest shortly after diagnosis and declines with time, although studies based on secondary psychiatric care have found excess mortality persisting during longer follow-up [16] [17] [18].
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that excess mortality following depression, anxiety, and stress-related disorders is highest shortly after diagnosis and declines with time, although studies based on secondary psychiatric care have found excess mortality persisting during longer follow-up <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Recent meta-analyses nevertheless show substantial variation according to the populations studied [8, 9].
text.formatted: Recent meta-analyses nevertheless show substantial variation according to the populations studied <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: For depression, mortality remains elevated in community samples, whereas an earlier meta-analysis found no excess mortality associated with anxiety in community samples [8, 19].
text.formatted: For depression, mortality remains elevated in community samples, whereas an earlier meta-analysis found no excess mortality associated with anxiety in community samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">19]</ref>.

text.text: Our findings bring these dimensions together by showing that the temporal pattern itself differs according to clinical context.

The persistent excess mortality observed in specialist psychiatric populations should therefore not be assumed to characterize the broader-and substantially largerpopulation with common mental disorders diagnosed outside specialist psychiatric care.
This difference also has implications for case ascertainment in mortality studies.
Previous studies have shown that mortality estimates based on specialist psychiatric populations may differ substantially from those in the broader population [10, 20, 21].
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that mortality estimates based on specialist psychiatric populations may differ substantially from those in the broader population <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">21]</ref>.

text.text: Our findings further show that the implications of restricting ascertainment to specialist psychiatric care vary across the life course.
Such restriction produced particularly high relative mortality estimates in young and middle-aged adults, but lower estimates at older ages than ascertainment from both primary and specialist care.

Thus, specialist psychiatric populations do not represent a uniformly higher-mortality subset of people with mental disorders, and their relationship to the broader diagnosed population changes with age.
Age also modified the temporal patterns within diagnostic groups.

Among individuals aged 65-95 years, depression was an important exception to the attenuation observed for common mental disorders at younger ages: excess mortality persisted across clinical subgroups, including among those without SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care.
A similar persistent pattern was not observed for anxiety or fear-related disorders.
Previous studies have consistently associated late-life depression with increased mortality in community populations [22].
text.formatted: Previous studies have consistently associated late-life depression with increased mortality in community populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Notably, in our study excess mortality persisted after adjustment for baseline physical comorbidity.

This distinct mortality trajectory is consistent with broader evidence that depression in later life differs from depression in younger adults in its clinical characteristics, prognosis, and relationships with physical and neurocognitive disorders [23].
text.formatted: This distinct mortality trajectory is consistent with broader evidence that depression in later life differs from depression in younger adults in its clinical characteristics, prognosis, and relationships with physical and neurocognitive disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[23]</ref>.

text.text: SUD was an important marker of mortality within diagnostic groups, consistent with the substantial excess mortality associated with SUD and co-occurring mental disorders reported previously [11, [24] [25] [26] [27].
text.formatted: SUD was an important marker of mortality within diagnostic groups, consistent with the substantial excess mortality associated with SUD and co-occurring mental disorders reported previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[27]</ref>.

text.text: However, SUD status alone did not distinguish transient from persistent excess mortality.

Among individuals with common mental disorders, excess mortality declined substantially among those with SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care, whereas it remained elevated among those receiving specialist psychiatric care even without SUD.

Treating SUD solely as a covariate may therefore obscure clinically important heterogeneity, as mortality trajectories differed substantially according to SUD status, clinical setting, and time since diagnosis even within the same diagnostic group.

These differences were also apparent on an absolute scale, with substantially greater tenyear survival loss among individuals with SUD and those receiving specialist psychiatric care than among those without SUD treated outside specialist psychiatric care.

Applying the ICD-11 framework classified fewer individuals as having a mental, behavioural, or neurodevelopmental disorder than ICD-10 main diagnostic groups and yielded higher overall MRRs, particularly when diagnoses outside specialist psychiatric care were included.
Thus, diagnostic classification can change both the population identified as having a mental disorder and the resulting estimate of the mortality gap.
This study has several limitations.

First, primary care data were available only from 2011, and some prevalent disorders may therefore have been misclassified as incident, although sensitivity analyses restricted to more recent diagnoses yielded similar results.
Second, ICD-11 diagnostic groups were derived from ICD-10 codes using WHO mapping tables rather than diagnoses recorded using ICD-11.
Third, SUDs are likely to be underascertained in health care registers, which may have reduced observed differences according to SUD status.

SUD status and psychiatric care setting should be interpreted as markers of clinical context rather than causal determinants of mortality; both may reflect disorder severity, other patient characteristics, and patterns of health care contact.
Fourth, time since diagnosis refers to time since the first recorded diagnosis.

The analyses could not establish when a disorder began or distinguish active disorder, remission, and recurrence, and the observed temporal patterns should therefore not be interpreted as effects of diagnosis itself.
Fifth, physical comorbidity was assessed at cohort entry and not updated during follow-up, so subsequent changes in physical health were not captured by CCI adjustment.

Finally, the ten-year RMST differences quantify survival lost during the first ten years after diagnosis and should not be interpreted as reductions in life expectancy or extrapolated beyond the observed follow-up.
In conclusion, the mortality gap associated with mental disorders cannot be adequately characterized by diagnostic group or a single summary estimate.

Excess mortality may be transient in large parts of the diagnosed population while remaining substantial or persistent in others with the same diagnosis, depending on time since diagnosis and clinical context.
Recognizing this heterogeneity may provide a stronger basis for targeting prevention and for giving patients and clinicians a more informative account of mortality after diagnosis.

Finland population data were linked using unique personal identity codes to the Care Register for Health Care and Register of Primary Health Care Visits maintained by the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL).
These registers include psychiatric inpatient care since 1975, specialist outpatient care since 1998, and public primary care since 2011 and have shown good coverage and diagnostic validity [12,13].
The study received favorable ethical review from the THL Institutional Review Board (decision #10/2016 §751), and data linkage was authorized by Statistics Finland (TK-53-1696-16) and THL.
Informed consent is not required for register-based studies in Finland.
Mental disorder diagnoses were treated as time-varying.
For each diagnostic group, individuals contributed person-time without the diagnosis until the first recorded diagnosis and with the diagnosis thereafter.

Following diagnosis, person-time was dynamically allocated to 4 mutually exclusive states according to psychiatric care setting and substance use disorder (SUD) status: outside specialist psychiatric care without SUD, outside specialist psychiatric care with SUD, specialist psychiatric care without SUD, and specialist psychiatric care with SUD.

Individuals entered the specialist-care state when the diagnosis was first recorded in specialist psychiatric care and the SUD state at first recorded SUD diagnosis; both classifications were cumulative.
Care outside specialist psychiatric care included primary care and nonpsychiatric specialist services.
SUD was defined as ICD-11 disorders due to substance use (6C4).
